titre: WorldCom Collapses, Congress Legislates Nine Days Later
accroche: On July 21, 2002, WorldCom files the largest bankruptcy in the country's history. Nine days later, a law requires every chief executive to personally sign off on the accounts.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 21, 2002, the telecom operator WorldCom files for bankruptcy with more than $100 billion in reported assets: the largest corporate bankruptcy in U.S. history at that point, ahead of Enron and its $63.4 billion in assets seven months earlier. On June 25, WorldCom had admitted to reclassifying about $3.8 billion in ordinary expenses as capital investments, to artificially inflate its profits; the very next day, the Securities and Exchange Commission sued the company for fraud. On July 30, 2002, nine days after WorldCom's bankruptcy filing, President George W. Bush signs at the White House a law that he describes, in his speech, as “the most far-reaching reforms of American business practices since the time of Franklin Delano Roosevelt.”

## Signing, Personally

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 targets a specific flaw exposed by Enron and WorldCom: in the chain that produced falsified accounts, no one was named as legally responsible. Its section 302 changes that. It requires the chief executive officer and the chief financial officer of every publicly traded company to personally certify, in writing, each quarterly and annual report filed with the regulator: that they have reviewed it themselves, that the accounts fairly present the company's financial condition, that they have established and assessed internal controls designed to bring any material information to their attention, and that they have disclosed to the auditors any weakness or fraud they know of. Another provision of the law, section 906, makes signing a certification one knows to be false an offense separate from the underlying accounting fraud, punishable by a fine of up to $5 million and twenty years in prison for a willful violation.

## The Shift

Before 2002, an executive could claim not to know what was going on in his own accounting department, and the law did not squarely contradict him: responsibility remained diluted among the board of directors, the outside auditors, and the finance teams. After section 302, ignorance ceases to be an admissible defense, since the executive has personally certified the opposite, under his own signature. The shift extends beyond U.S. borders: any subsidiary of a group listed in the United States, wherever it is located, now feeds this same chain of internal certifications that runs up to a single signature. Holding a named individual accountable, rather than the company as an abstract entity, has since become a principle taken up by most financial compliance laws written after it.

carte.punch: Nine days after the biggest bankruptcy to date, executives must certify the accounts.
carte.idee: On July 21, 2002, WorldCom files for bankruptcy with more than $100 billion in reported assets, then the largest corporate bankruptcy in the United States. On July 30, the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires the chief executive and chief financial officer of every publicly traded company to certify the accounts.

quiz.question: What does section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act concretely change compared with the situation before 2002?
choix: The chief executive and the chief financial officer must personally certify in writing that they have reviewed the company's accounts and internal controls
Companies must now have their accounts audited by an outside firm, which was not mandatory before
Congress takes direct control of the accounting of large publicly traded companies
Shareholders can now sue the company without going through the Securities and Exchange Commission
quiz.explication: External audits already existed before 2002 and the SEC remained the competent regulator; what section 302 introduces is a personal, written certification that engages the executive's own responsibility, rather than that of the company alone. The criminal penalty for a knowingly false certification, up to 20 years in prison, comes from a separate provision of the law, section 906.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did WorldCom admit on June 25, 2002, the day before the SEC filed its complaint?
choix: That it had reclassified about $3.8 billion in expenses as capital investments
That it had paid bribes to its outside auditors to hide its losses
That it had concealed a merger with a competitor without informing shareholders
That it had falsified its subscriber numbers to reassure the markets
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On June 25, 2002, WorldCom admits to reclassifying about $3.8 billion in expenses as capital investments, which artificially inflates its reported profits.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Whom does section 302 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act require to personally certify financial reports?
choix: The entire board of directors, collectively
The chief executive officer and the chief financial officer
The outside audit firm in charge of the accounts
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 302 names the chief executive officer and the chief financial officer, who must personally sign a written certification for each report filed.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does section 906 add to the certification requirement of section 302?
choix: It extends the personal certification requirement to companies not listed on the stock market as well
It requires the SEC to inspect every report systematically each quarter
It caps the annual pay of executives who have signed a certification
It makes signing a knowingly false certification a separate offense, punishable by twenty years in prison
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 302 creates the obligation to certify; section 906 is a separate criminal provision, which punishes signing a certification one knows to be false.
